(ii) Three point charges q, 2q and nq are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. If the potential energy of the system is zero, find the value of n.
rows.solution:
(i) POTENTIAL DUE TO A SHORT DIPOLE.
Let the dipole consist of \(-q\) at A and \(+q\) at B, separated by \(2a\), with centre O. Let P be a point at distance r from O, the line OP making an angle \(\theta\) with the dipole axis. Write \(r_{1}\) and \(r_{2}\) for the distances from \(+q\) and \(-q\) to P.
THE EXACT POTENTIAL is the scalar sum of the two contributions:
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left(\dfrac{q}{r_{1}} - \dfrac{q}{r_{2}}\right) \qquad \ldots(1)\)
THE GEOMETRY. By the cosine rule applied to the two triangles,
\(r_{1}^{2} = r^{2} + a^{2} - 2ar\cos\theta \qquad r_{2}^{2} = r^{2} + a^{2} + 2ar\cos\theta\)
FOR \(r \gg a\), the term \(a^{2}\) is negligible beside \(r^{2}\), so
\(r_{1}^{2} \approx r^{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{2a\cos\theta}{r}\right) \qquad r_{2}^{2} \approx r^{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{2a\cos\theta}{r}\right)\)
Taking the inverse square root of each and expanding binomially, keeping only the first order in \(\dfrac{a}{r}\):
\(\dfrac{1}{r_{1}} \approx \dfrac{1}{r}\left(1 + \dfrac{a\cos\theta}{r}\right) \qquad \dfrac{1}{r_{2}} \approx \dfrac{1}{r}\left(1 - \dfrac{a\cos\theta}{r}\right)\)
SUBSTITUTING into (1), the two 1's cancel and the two \(\dfrac{a\cos\theta}{r}\) terms ADD:
\(V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left(\dfrac{2a\cos\theta}{r^{2}}\right)\)
Writing the dipole moment \(p = q(2a)\):
\(V = \dfrac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\)
Two features are characteristic of a dipole. The potential falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\), faster than a point charge's \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), because the two opposite charges very nearly cancel at a distance. And it depends on DIRECTION through \(\cos\theta\): maximum along the axis, and ZERO everywhere on the equatorial plane, where \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) and the two charges are equidistant.
(ii) FINDING n.
The potential energy of three charges is the sum over the three PAIRS, and in an equilateral triangle of side a every pair is the same distance apart:
\(U = \dfrac{k}{a}\left[q_{1}q_{2} + q_{2}q_{3} + q_{1}q_{3}\right]\)
With the charges q, 2q and nq:
\(U = \dfrac{k}{a}\left[(q)(2q) + (2q)(nq) + (q)(nq)\right] = \dfrac{kq^{2}}{a}\left[2 + 2n + n\right]\)
Setting the total energy to zero, and noting that \(\dfrac{kq^{2}}{a}\) cannot itself vanish:
\(2 + 3n = 0\)
\(n = -\dfrac{2}{3}\)
The value is NEGATIVE, as it had to be. The first pair q and 2q are both positive and repel, contributing positive energy; the only way the total can come to zero is for the third charge to be of OPPOSITE sign, so that its two attractions cancel that contribution exactly.

rows.stem:
(i) State Gauss's Law in electrostatics. Apply this to obtain the electric field \(\vec{E}\) at a point near a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
(ii) Two long straight wires 1 and 2 are kept as shown in the figure. The linear charge density of the two wires are \(\lambda_1 = 10\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\) and \(\lambda_2 = -20\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\). Find the net force \(\vec{F}\) experienced by an electron held at point P.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (ii) is unanswerable from its stem: every distance lives only in the drawing. Two horizontal parallel lines, the upper labelled 1 at its left end and \(\lambda_1\) at its right, the lower labelled 2 and \(\lambda_2\); a vertical dimension arrow at the left marks 30 cm between them, and a second arrow marks 10 cm between the upper wire and the point P, which is drawn as a labelled dot between the wires. A separate \(\hat{i}\)/\(\hat{j}\) axis key sits to the right, \(\hat{j}\) upward and \(\hat{i}\) rightward. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) GAUSS'S LAW AND THE INFINITE CHARGED SHEET.
STATEMENT. The total electric flux through any CLOSED surface is \(\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}}\) times the total charge ENCLOSED by that surface:
\(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = \dfrac{q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
APPLYING IT TO THE SHEET. Let the plane sheet carry a uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). By symmetry the field must be perpendicular to the sheet and of the same magnitude at equal distances on either side.
Choose as the Gaussian surface a CYLINDER (or rectangular box) pierced symmetrically by the sheet, with its flat end faces of area A parallel to the sheet, one on each side.
THE FLUX. The CURVED side contributes nothing, because there \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to the surface and \(\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = 0\). Only the two END FACES contribute, and at each the field is along the outward normal, so their contributions ADD:
\(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S} = EA + EA = 2EA\)
THE CHARGE ENCLOSED is that on the intercepted patch of sheet:
\(q_{enclosed} = \sigma A\)
Equating by Gauss's law:
\(2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
The area A cancels — which is what tells us the field is independent of how far away we are:
\(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\hat{n}\)
where \(\hat{n}\) is the unit vector directed normally away from the sheet (towards it if \(\sigma\) is negative). The field is UNIFORM, the same at every distance, which is the striking feature of an infinite sheet.
(ii) THE NET FORCE ON THE ELECTRON AT P.
The field of a long straight charged wire at perpendicular distance r is
\(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\hat{r}\)
FIELD DUE TO WIRE 1, with \(\lambda_{1} = +10\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\) at \(r_{1} = 10\) cm. Being POSITIVE, its field points AWAY from the wire, which from the figure is the \(-\hat{j}\) direction:
\(\vec{E}_{1} = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(10 \times 10^{-2}\right)}\left(-\hat{j}\right)\)
FIELD DUE TO WIRE 2, with \(\lambda_{2} = -20\ \mu\mathrm{C/m}\) at \(r_{2} = 20\) cm. Being NEGATIVE, its field points TOWARDS that wire — which from the figure is also \(-\hat{j}\):
\(\vec{E}_{2} = \dfrac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\left(20 \times 10^{-2}\right)}\left(-\hat{j}\right)\)
The two point the SAME way and therefore add:
\(\vec{E}_{net} = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left(\dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}1} + \dfrac{2}{0{\cdot}2}\right)\left(-\hat{j}\right) = \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-6}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left(20\right)\left(-\hat{j}\right)\)
\(\vec{E}_{net} = 3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6}\left(-\hat{j}\right)\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\)
THE FORCE ON THE ELECTRON, of charge \(-1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\) C:
\(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}_{net} = \left(-1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(3{\cdot}6 \times 10^{6}\right)\left(-\hat{j}\right)\)
\(\vec{F} = 5{\cdot}76 \times 10^{-13}\ \hat{j}\ \mathrm{N}\)
The two minus signs — one from the electron's charge, one from the field's direction — cancel, so the force on the electron is directed along \(+\hat{j}\), OPPOSITE to the field, as it must be for a negative charge.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
(i) A particle of mass m and charge q is moving with a velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) as shown in the figure. Show that it follows a helical path. Hence, obtain its frequency of revolution.
(ii) In a hydrogen atom, the electron moves in an orbit of radius \(2\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) making \(8 \times 10^{14}\) revolutions per second. Find the magnetic moment associated with the orbital motion of the electron.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (i) says 'as shown in the figure' and states no directions at all. A right-handed set of axes x (rightward), y (upward) and z (toward the lower left); an arrow labelled \(\vec{B}\) and an arrow labelled \(\vec{v}\) are both drawn in the upper-right region. The ORIENTATION of \(\vec{v}\) relative to \(\vec{B}\) is withheld here: that the two are oblique rather than parallel or perpendicular is the whole premise of 'show that it follows a helical path'. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
(i) THE HELICAL PATH AND THE FREQUENCY.
RESOLVING THE VELOCITY. Let \(\vec{v}\) make an angle \(\theta\) with \(\vec{B}\), and split it into two components:
\(v_{\perp} = v\sin\theta \quad\text{perpendicular to}\ \vec{B} \qquad v_{\parallel} = v\cos\theta \quad\text{parallel to}\ \vec{B}\)
WHAT EACH COMPONENT DOES. The magnetic force is \(q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\), so the PARALLEL component contributes nothing — \(\vec{v}_{\parallel} \times \vec{B} = 0\) — and that part of the motion continues unchanged, carrying the particle steadily along the field direction.
The PERPENDICULAR component feels the full force and, being always perpendicular to the velocity, drives uniform CIRCULAR motion in the plane normal to \(\vec{B}\).
A uniform circular motion superposed on a uniform drift along the axis of that circle is a HELIX. Its radius is set by \(v_{\perp}\) and its PITCH — the distance advanced per revolution — by \(v_{\parallel}\).
THE FREQUENCY. For the circular part, the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force:
\(\dfrac{mv_{\perp}^{2}}{r} = qv_{\perp}B \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_{\perp} = \dfrac{Bqr}{m}\)
The period is the circumference divided by the speed round it:
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v_{\perp}} = \dfrac{2\pi r m}{Bqr} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{Bq}\)
\(\nu = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{Bq}{2\pi m}\)
Both r and \(v_{\perp}\) have cancelled, so the frequency does NOT depend on the speed or on the angle \(\theta\) — a faster particle simply travels a proportionally larger circle in the same time. This is the cyclotron frequency, and its independence of speed is exactly what allows a cyclotron to accelerate particles with a fixed-frequency supply.
(ii) THE MAGNETIC MOMENT OF THE ORBITING ELECTRON.
THE EQUIVALENT CURRENT. An electron making \(\nu\) revolutions per second carries charge e past any point on the orbit \(\nu\) times per second:
\(I = \dfrac{e}{T} = e\nu = \left(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right)\left(8 \times 10^{14}\right)\)
\(I = 1{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{A}\)
THE AREA of the orbit, with \(r = 2\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} = 2 \times 10^{-10}\) m:
\(A = \pi r^{2} = 3{\cdot}14 \times \left(2 \times 10^{-10}\right)^{2} = 1{\cdot}256 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)
THE MAGNETIC MOMENT:
\(M = IA = \left(1{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-4}\right)\left(1{\cdot}256 \times 10^{-19}\right)\)
\(M \approx 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{2}}\)
The value is close to the Bohr magneton, \(9{\cdot}27 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{2}}\), which is the natural unit of atomic magnetism — reassuring, since an electron circling an atom at atomic dimensions is precisely what that unit describes.

rows.stem:
(i) What is current sensitivity of a galvanometer ? Show how the current sensitivity of a galvanometer may be increased. "Increasing the current sensitivity of a galvanometer may not necessarily increase its voltage sensitivity." Explain.
(ii) A moving coil galvanometer has a resistance \(15\ \Omega\) and takes 20 mA to produce full scale deflection. How can this galvanometer be converted into a voltmeter of range 0 to 100 V ?
rows.solution:
(i) CURRENT SENSITIVITY.
DEFINITION. The current sensitivity of a galvanometer is the DEFLECTION PRODUCED PER UNIT CURRENT:
\(I_{s} = \dfrac{\varphi}{I} = \dfrac{NBA}{k}\)
where N is the number of turns, B the radial field, A the coil's area and k the torsional constant of the suspension.
HOW TO INCREASE IT. Any factor that raises the numerator or lowers the denominator will serve:
INCREASE THE NUMBER OF TURNS N in the coil;
INCREASE THE AREA A of the coil (or the field strength B);
DECREASE THE TORSIONAL CONSTANT k, by using a finer or more flexible suspension.
WHY VOLTAGE SENSITIVITY NEED NOT FOLLOW. The voltage sensitivity is the deflection per unit VOLTAGE across the galvanometer:
\(V_{s} = \dfrac{\varphi}{V} = \dfrac{\varphi}{IR} = \dfrac{NBA}{kR}\)
where R is the galvanometer's own resistance. The two sensitivities differ by that factor of R, and that is the whole point.
Suppose the current sensitivity is raised by INCREASING N. More turns means more WIRE, and more wire means a larger resistance R. Both N and R therefore increase together, and since N is in the numerator of \(V_{s}\) while R is in the denominator, the two changes tend to CANCEL. The voltage sensitivity may rise a little, stay the same, or even fall.
So the two are independent measures, and improving one is not automatically improving the other. (Increasing the AREA, by contrast, raises N-independent sensitivity without adding much resistance, and is the better route if voltage sensitivity matters.)
(ii) CONVERTING THE GALVANOMETER INTO A VOLTMETER.
To read up to V volts, a HIGH resistance R must be connected in SERIES, so that the full-scale current \(I_{G}\) flows when V is applied across the combination:
\(V = I_{G}(R + G) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R = \dfrac{V}{I_{G}} - G\)
Substituting \(V = 100\) V, \(I_{G} = 20\ \mathrm{mA} = 20 \times 10^{-3}\) A and \(G = 15\ \Omega\):
\(R = \dfrac{100}{20 \times 10^{-3}} - 15 = 5000 - 15\)
\(R = 4985\ \Omega\)
So connecting a resistance of \(4985\ \Omega\) IN SERIES with the galvanometer converts it into a voltmeter reading 0 to 100 V.
The series connection is essential for two reasons: it limits the current to the full-scale value, and it makes the instrument's total resistance very LARGE — 5000 Ω against the galvanometer's 15 Ω — so that connecting it across a circuit element draws almost no current and disturbs the circuit as little as possible. An ammeter needs the opposite treatment, a small shunt in parallel.

rows.stem:
(i) Give any two differences between the interference pattern obtained in Young's double-slit experiment and a diffraction pattern due to a single slit.
(ii) Draw an intensity distribution graph in case of a double-slit interference pattern.
(iii) In Young's double-slit experiment using monochromatic light of wavelength \(\lambda\), the intensity of light at a point on the screen, where path difference is \(\lambda\), is K units. Find the intensity of light at a point on the screen where the path difference is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{6}\).
rows.solution:
(i) TWO DIFFERENCES BETWEEN INTERFERENCE AND DIFFRACTION (any two):
FRINGE SPACING. In an interference pattern the bands are EQUALLY SPACED. In a diffraction pattern they are NOT — the central maximum is twice as wide as the others, and the spacing is irregular thereafter.
INTENSITY OF THE MAXIMA. In interference all the bright bands have the SAME intensity. In diffraction the intensity of the maxima FALLS OFF rapidly on either side of the central maximum, the first secondary maximum being only about 4% of it.
POSITION OF THE FIRST FEATURE. In interference the first MAXIMUM occurs at an angle \(\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\) (with a the slit separation). In diffraction the first MINIMUM occurs at \(\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\) (with a the slit width) — a maximum in one case, a minimum in the other.
(ii) INTENSITY DISTRIBUTION FOR DOUBLE-SLIT INTERFERENCE.
Plot intensity against path difference. The graph is a succession of identical peaks of EQUAL height \(I_{max}\), evenly spaced, with maxima at path differences \(0, \pm\lambda, \pm 2\lambda, \pm 3\lambda, \ldots\) and zeros exactly midway between them. The curve is \(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}\), rising and falling smoothly between \(4I_{0}\) and 0, with every peak the same height — which is the visual signature that distinguishes it from a diffraction pattern.
(iii) FINDING THE INTENSITY.
The intensity in a two-slit pattern is
\(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2} \qquad\text{with}\qquad \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \Delta\)
FIRST, CALIBRATE K. At a path difference \(\Delta = \lambda\):
\(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \lambda = 2\pi\)
\(K = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\pi = 4I_{0}(1) = 4I_{0}\)
So the point given is in fact a bright fringe at FULL intensity, and \(4I_{0} = K\).
NOW THE POINT ASKED FOR, at \(\Delta = \dfrac{\lambda}{6}\):
\(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)
\(I = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{6} = 4I_{0}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2} = 4I_{0} \times \dfrac{3}{4}\)
Substituting \(4I_{0} = K\):
\(I = \dfrac{3}{4}K\)
The calibration step is what the question is built around: the intensity K is not the intensity of one slit but of a MAXIMUM, since a path difference of a whole wavelength puts the waves back in step. A reader who takes K as \(I_{0}\) arrives at 3K instead, which exceeds the maximum the pattern can produce.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a labelled ray diagram of a compound microscope showing image formation at least distance of distinct vision. Derive an expression for its magnifying power.
(ii) A telescope consists of two lenses of focal length 100 cm and 5 cm. Find the magnifying power when the final image is formed at infinity.
rows.solution:
(i) THE COMPOUND MICROSCOPE.
THE RAY DIAGRAM. Draw two converging lenses on a common axis: the OBJECTIVE of short focal length \(f_{o}\) and the EYEPIECE of focal length \(f_{e}\). Place the object AB just BEYOND the objective's focus, so the objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image \(A'B'\) inside the tube. Position the eyepiece so that \(A'B'\) falls just INSIDE its focal length; the eyepiece then acts as a simple magnifier, and the final image \(A''B''\) is formed at the LEAST DISTANCE OF DISTINCT VISION D, on the same side as the object, virtual and inverted with respect to the original. Mark \(f_{o}\), \(f_{e}\), \(u_{o}\), \(v_{o}\) and D, with arrows on every ray.
THE MAGNIFYING POWER. Each lens contributes, and the two MULTIPLY because the eyepiece magnifies what the objective has already produced.
MAGNIFICATION BY THE OBJECTIVE, a straightforward linear magnification:
\(m_{o} = \dfrac{v_{o}}{-u_{o}}\)
MAGNIFICATION BY THE EYEPIECE, used as a simple magnifier with the final image at the near point:
\(m_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\)
TOTAL MAGNIFYING POWER:
\(m = m_{o} \times m_{e}\)
\(m = \dfrac{v_{o}}{-u_{o}}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\right)\)
Both focal lengths need to be SHORT for a large magnification — the objective's to give a large \(\dfrac{v_{o}}{u_{o}}\), the eyepiece's to give a large \(\dfrac{D}{f_{e}}\). That is the opposite of a telescope, whose objective must have a LONG focal length, and it is the structural difference between the two instruments.
(ii) THE TELESCOPE'S MAGNIFYING POWER.
For an astronomical telescope with the final image at INFINITY (normal adjustment),
\(m = \left|\dfrac{f_{o}}{f_{e}}\right|\)
The two lenses are of focal lengths 100 cm and 5 cm. The OBJECTIVE must be the one of LONGER focal length — it is what gathers light from the distant object and forms the intermediate image — so \(f_{o} = 100\) cm and \(f_{e} = 5\) cm:
\(m = \dfrac{100}{5}\)
\(m = 20\)
The magnifying power is 20.
Identifying which lens is which is the step that matters: taking them the other way round would give \(\dfrac{1}{20}\), a telescope that made things smaller. For completeness, the tube length in this adjustment is \(f_{o} + f_{e} = 105\) cm, which is why a high-power refracting telescope is necessarily a long instrument.
